# 01 — Synthetic Data Generation

## Concept

RAG demos need a corpus that is realistic enough to produce meaningful
retrieval and reranking behavior, but that raises zero privacy, licensing,
or confidentiality concerns. The standard trick — used here — is
**synthetic data**: text generated by a fake-data library (Faker) and woven
into domain-flavored templates, then rendered into the same file formats a
real deployment would ingest (PDF, CSV).

Why synthetic data is the right choice for teaching RAG:

- **No real customer/employee/financial data anywhere.** Every name, dollar
  amount, date, and account number is fabricated. You can share this
  project, screenshot it, or put it in a public repo without a compliance
  review.
- **Reproducibility.** A fixed random seed (`cfg.corpus.seed`, default `42`)
  means everyone who runs `generate_all()` gets byte-for-byte the same
  corpus, so lesson output ("chunk 3 of file X should look like...") is
  stable across machines.
- **Structural realism.** The generators don't just emit lorem-ipsum — they
  produce documents with headings, sections, tables, and a controlled
  vocabulary of banking terms (`BANKING_VOCAB` in `common.py`), so semantic
  search and reranking have genuine topical signal to work with instead of
  random noise.
- **Volume control.** `config.yaml`'s `corpus.num_pdfs` / `num_sops` /
  `num_csvs` let you dial the corpus size up or down to see how retrieval
  quality and chunk counts change.

## In this repo

All generation code lives under `src/data_gen/`:

- `src/data_gen/common.py`
  - `DISCLAIMER`, `DISCLAIMER_LONG`, `FOOTER_DISCLAIMER` — the disclaimer
    strings stamped onto every generated document (title page, footer, and
    a standalone `DISCLAIMER.txt` for the CSVs).
  - `seed_all(seed)` — seeds Python's `random` module and Faker together so
    a full generation run is reproducible; returns a `Faker("en_US")`
    instance.
  - `banking_sentence(fake)` / `banking_paragraph(fake, min_sentences, max_sentences)`
    — combine a Faker-generated sentence with a banking-domain template
    drawn from `_TEMPLATES`, using a topic sampled from `BANKING_VOCAB`
    (e.g. "wire transfer authorization", "KYC verification"). This is what
    makes the generated paragraphs read as topical banking prose instead of
    pure lorem ipsum.
  - `CascadePDF(FPDF)` — an `fpdf2` subclass with a Cascade Bank title page,
    a disclaimer footer on every page (`CascadePDF.footer`), and helper
    methods: `add_title_page`, `add_heading`, `add_paragraphs`, `add_section`,
    `add_numbered_list`, `add_key_value_table`, `add_simple_table`.
  - `slugify(text)` — turns a document title into a filesystem-safe
    filename fragment.

- `src/data_gen/generate_pdfs.py`
  - `generate_pdfs(n=None) -> list[Path]` — writes `cfg.corpus.num_pdfs`
    (default 18) policy/manual PDFs into `cfg.paths.pdfs`
    (`data/raw/pdfs/`). Titles are drawn from `POLICY_TITLES` (10 policy
    docs, e.g. "Account Overdraft Policy") and `MANUAL_TITLES` (8 product
    manuals, e.g. "Mobile Banking App Manual"); each becomes `doc_type`
    `"policy"` or `"manual"` at generation time (note: by the time chunks
    reach Chroma, `doc_type` is normalized to the coarser `"pdf"` /
    `"sop"` / `"csv"` used everywhere downstream — see
    `src/ingest/chunk.py:_doc_type_for_path`). Each document gets 2-4
    randomly sampled sections (from `POLICY_SECTIONS` or `MANUAL_SECTIONS`)
    with 4-12 banking-flavored paragraphs each.

- `src/data_gen/generate_sops.py`
  - `generate_sops(n=None) -> list[Path]` — writes `cfg.corpus.num_sops`
    (default 8) Standard Operating Procedure PDFs into `cfg.paths.sops`
    (`data/raw/sops/`). Every SOP has a **fixed structure**: Title →
    Purpose → Scope → Procedure Steps (a numbered list drawn from
    `STEP_ACTIONS`) → Roles & Responsibilities (a key/value table from
    `ROLE_POOL`) → Revision History (a fabricated version table via
    `_fake_revision_history`). Topics come from `SOP_TOPICS` (e.g.
    "Suspicious Activity Reporting", "Wire Transfer Authorization").

- `src/data_gen/generate_csvs.py`
  - `generate_csvs(n=None) -> list[Path]` — writes up to `cfg.corpus.num_csvs`
    (default 5, clamped to the 5 available schemas) CSVs into `cfg.paths.csvs`
    (`data/raw/csvs/`): `employee_directory.csv`, `transaction_log.csv`,
    `support_tickets.csv`, `branch_inventory.csv`, `loan_portfolio.csv`.
    Each schema has its own builder function (e.g. `_employee_directory`,
    `_transaction_log`) using `pandas.DataFrame.to_csv`. A shared
    `DISCLAIMER.txt` is written alongside them via `_write_disclaimer`.

- `src/data_gen/generate_all.py`
  - `generate_all() -> dict[str, int]` — calls `generate_pdfs()`,
    `generate_sops()`, `generate_csvs()` in order and prints/returns a
    summary `{"pdfs": n, "sops": n, "csvs": n}`.

## Try it

Generate just the PDFs (fast, isolates one generator):

```powershell
python -m src.data_gen.generate_pdfs
```

Generate the full corpus and see the summary:

```powershell
python -m src.data_gen.generate_all
```

Open one generated PDF (e.g. the first one printed) in a PDF viewer and
confirm you can see the red **"SYNTHETIC / FICTIONAL DEMO DATA — NOT A REAL
BANK"** banner on the title page, plus the smaller disclaimer footer on
every subsequent page.

## What to look for / checkpoint

- `data/raw/pdfs/` contains 18 files named like
  `01_policy_account_overdraft_policy.pdf` or
  `05_manual_mobile_banking_app_manual.pdf`.
- `data/raw/sops/` contains 8 files named like
  `01_sop_new_account_opening.pdf`.
- `data/raw/csvs/` contains exactly 5 CSVs plus `DISCLAIMER.txt`.
- Re-running any generator with the same `cfg.corpus.seed` reproduces
  byte-identical output (check file sizes/hashes if in doubt) — this is the
  reproducibility guarantee `seed_all()` provides.
- Every PDF's title page shows the disclaimer banner; every page footer
  reads "Cascade Bank (fictional) — synthetic demo data, not a real
  institution — Page N".

## Teaching note

Point trainees at `BANKING_VOCAB` and `_TEMPLATES` in `common.py` and have
them add one new vocabulary term and one new template sentence, then
re-generate and diff the output — it's a fast, safe way to see exactly how
much of the "realism" in these documents is template scaffolding versus
Faker randomness. This also previews a recurring theme of the course: small,
inspectable pieces compose into a corpus that's good enough to make
retrieval and reranking behave meaningfully differently, without needing any
real text at all.
